title: The King's Bad Omen at Sunrise (HI)
summary: Akbar encounters an ugly sweeper at sunrise and fears an evil omen. Birbal shows the Emperor that the sweeper is the true benefactor of the city.
full_text:
Early one morning, Emperor Akbar stepped out onto the east-facing terrace to perform his morning devotions at sunrise. Just as the golden rim of the sun crested the horizon, Akbar looked down into the courtyard and his eyes fell upon a municipal sweeper named Kalu—an impoverished, one-eyed man in ragged clothes carrying a broom of twigs and a basket of horse dung.

Akbar turned back in dismay: 'What an ill-omened sight! To see an ugly sweeper with a basket of dung at the very moment of sunrise! This day will bring misfortune to the empire!'

Later that morning, during the council assembly, Akbar was irritable and nervous, jumping at every noise.

Birbal noticed the Emperor's distress and inquired: 'Sire, why are you troubled today?'

Akbar explained: 'At sunrise, the first creature I saw was an ugly sweeper carrying a basket of dung! My day is cursed!'

Birbal smiled gently, stepped out, and brought the sweeper Kalu into the Diwan-i-Am. The poor man was trembling with fear, clutching his broom.

Birbal said to the Emperor:

'Your Majesty, you consider Kalu an evil omen because he carries a basket of waste.

'Yet consider what would happen to your magnificent capital if Kalu and his fellow sweepers stayed home for just one single week!

'The streets of Agra would be choked with filth, disease and pestilence would sweep through every household, and the imperial palace itself would become unlivable!

'This humble man cleans away the filth of our lives so that we may breathe clean air and walk on clean stones! His labor is an act of pure public service.

'A corrupt minister who smiles with a handsome face while stealing public gold is the true evil omen! A humble sweeper who works honestly at sunrise to keep your city pure is a blessing from heaven!'

Akbar looked at the trembling sweeper, felt deep shame for his superstition, and stepped down from the dais.

Akbar placed a purse of fifty gold mohurs into the sweeper's calloused hands, granted him a warm woolen coat, and vowed never to judge human beings by superstition again.
